Guests can also order the Fantastic Flight, which includes four miniature cocktails featuring different flavors inspired by Marvel superheroes.

For those looking for alcohol-free options, Panther’s Potion combines cherry, ginger beer, and citrus sour with a blue shimmer sidecar, while Captain Punch features blue raspberry, coconut, pineapple, and lemon-lime soda.

All five beverages will be available from November 16 through January 31.

The promotion also includes a new event called DOOMHOUR, which gives D&B Rewards members the opportunity to earn double tickets on green-swipe games during randomly selected one-hour periods.

Members will receive a notification through the D&B Rewards app 24 hours before the next DOOMHOUR, followed by another notification revealing the exact time on the day of the event.

“When one of the biggest movies of the year is coming, you don’t put up a poster. You bend the knee,” said Jeremy Tucker, Chief Marketing Officer at Dave & Buster’s.

“We gave Doom our name. We gave him the floor. We gave him the bar. Doom & Buster’s is a world fans can only walk into with us, and it’s built for the thing we do better than anyone: bringing people together to play, compete, and be part of the action.”

Dave & Buster’s isn’t the only chain celebrating the upcoming Marvel movie. KFC also announced an Avengers: Doomsday collaboration featuring black burgers, green mayo, themed drinks, and collectible figurines. However, while the KFC promotion will launch in more than 100 countries beginning November 9, it won’t be available in the US.

#10775. Wendy’s free RPG rewards players with real food for beating bosses and is 15 hours long

Wendy’s has officially launched its free RPG, and somehow, the fast-food chain has created a game longer than some AAA blockbusters, complete with boss battles that reward players with actual food.

When WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones was first announced, the biggest surprise was that Wendy’s was making a full-blown, Final Fantasy-style RPG.

As it turns out, the company wasn’t messing around.

According to Wendy’s official website, the free-to-play adventure clocks in at approximately 15 hours of gameplay, featuring over 1,000 lines of dialogue.

For comparison, that’s more than double the length of some AAA campaigns such as Wolverine, which can be finished in 13 hours.

That’s an absurd amount of content for a game about a redheaded burger mascot fighting the forces of frozen beef.

Wendy’s has confirmed that players can unlock real-world food offers by defeating five bosses throughout the adventure.

Each boss provides a chance to earn a reward code redeemable through the Wendy’s app, with prizes including free medium fries, a small Frosty, 10-piece chicken nuggets, a breakfast biscuit or croissant, and even a Dave’s Single burger.

There is, however, a catch. Every food reward requires a separate purchase, and codes are available on a first-come, first-served basis while supplies last. Rewards are also restricted to US residents aged 18 and older.

Still, getting a burger for defeating an RPG boss is certainly a more delicious incentive than unlocking another achievement.

As for the game itself, WendyQuest features turn-based combat, puzzles, and five food-themed regions as players attempt to save the kingdom of Savoria from the villainous Dr. Mechborg.

#10771. Pro wrestler who plays evil politician elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island

A professional wrestler who portrays a corrupt politician in the ring has been elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, proving that sometimes the bad guy really does win.

David Morales, a 28-year-old Democrat and state representative, defeated Republican Dave Talan in the November 3 election, securing approximately 81% of the vote compared to his opponent’s 17%.

According to Rhode Island Current, Morales will become the youngest mayor in Providence history when he takes office in January 2027.

However, his political career isn’t the only thing that makes him stand out. Morales also happens to be a three-time wrestling champion who plays an evil politician.

Independent professional wrestler David Morales was elected mayor of Providence, Rhode Island in last night’s midterm elections pic.twitter.com/vFjAIABtlQ

Since 2021, Morales has competed in Rhode Island’s Renegade Wrestling Alliance under the name “The Commissioner,” portraying an arrogant political authority figure who loves getting under the crowd’s skin.

He’s even won the promotion’s Hype Championship three times, and once introduced a fictional rule requiring the champion to carry their title belt everywhere, including the statehouse.

In an October 2025 interview with Ocean State Media, Morales discussed the similarities between his two careers.

“I think there’s a lot of overlap,” he said. “Including showmanship, theater, athleticism, drama and humor.”

Ironically, Morales believes politicians have actually started taking too much inspiration from professional wrestling, warning that copying the exaggerated promos of WWE stars can lead to extremist rhetoric.

His wrestling career even became a talking point during the election campaign.

According to The Boston Globe, political opponents distributed campaign materials featuring Morales in his wrestling attire, accusing him of being “all hype, no results.”

Man wins election after telling voters he’s “unqualified” and has no idea what he’s doing

Seth Rollins’ next fight: Logan Paul, Roman Reigns among options for former champion

WWE Legend Kane reignites Die Hard Christmas movie debate and he’s not backing down

Clearly, voters weren’t particularly bothered by his extracurricular activities.

Morales announced his semi-retirement from wrestling while pursuing the mayor’s office, but hasn’t ruled out stepping back into the ring.

“Never say never in the world of professional wrestling,” he said.

Of course, Morales isn’t the first wrestler to trade the squared circle for public office.

WWE legend Kane, whose real name is Glenn Jacobs, was elected mayor of Knox County, Tennessee, which includes Knoxville, in 2018. He served until 2026 and even found time to reignite the debate over whether Die Hard is a Christmas movie while in office.

Former WWE star Jesse Ventura also famously became governor of Minnesota in 1999.

With Morales now heading to City Hall, Providence residents will have to wait and see whether The Commissioner makes an appearance during his time in office.

#10768. 8 Checks Developers Should Add Before Importing PDF Tables into an Application

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A PDF table can look correct and still produce unreliable application data. A wrapped description becomes two rows. An account code loses its leading zeros. A repeated page header is imported as a transaction. A missing decimal separator changes an amount without triggering an obvious error.

These problems are easy to overlook when an exported spreadsheet opens successfully. But opening a workbook proves very little about whether its contents belong in a database.

For developers building reporting dashboards, inventory systems, or document-import features, PDF extraction should feed a validation workflow. The following eight checks help separate readable output from data your application can safely process.

The examples use fictional invoice-style records and Python. They demonstrate a narrow validation contract rather than a complete PDF conversion service.

Not all PDFs contain the same kind of information.

A digitally generated document may include selectable text and vector lines. A scanned document may contain only page images. A mixed document can contain both, sometimes with an existing OCR layer that is incomplete or inaccurate.

Inspect representative pages before committing to an extraction strategy. Check whether text is selectable, whether copied Check parsing and validation behavior against fixtures

The pdfplumber documentation explains its text and table capabilities, including visual debugging. Its strengths are primarily associated with machine-generated PDFs; it is not an OCR engine.

OCRmyPDF adds a searchable text layer to scans. That does not, by itself, reconstruct a correct table schema. You still need to determine which text belongs in each row and column.

Practical check: Build a sample set containing a clean digital PDF, a scan, and a multi-page table before evaluating the extraction path.

A conversion step should create an inspectable intermediate result. It should not automatically authorize database writes.

For workflows that need a spreadsheet as the intermediate format, Lido is one option for converting PDF content to Excel. Evaluate the output against representative documents, then apply the same schema and reconciliation checks you would use with a custom extraction script.

Commit accepted records to the application.

This structure lets you replace an extraction tool without changing every downstream rule. It also provides a place to inspect failures before they become production records.

SitePoint’s guide to parsing spreadsheet data with Python provides background on working with spreadsheet formats in an application workflow.

Practical check: The importer should be able to reject a workbook even when conversion completed successfully.

Column names alone are not a sufficient contract. A field called “Date” could represent an invoice date, payment date, or service date.

Decide how repeated headers, subtotal rows, footnotes, and blank lines will be identified. Do not let them disappear through undocumented cleanup rules.

Load a workbook with deliberate type handling

The pandas read_excel reference documents these loading options. Using strings limits unwanted interpretation at this stage, while keep_default_na=False preserves values that would otherwise match default missing-value markers.

However, reading a cell as text cannot recover information already lost upstream. If a converter stored 00127 as the number 127, this setting will not reconstruct the original ID.

Practical check: Compare identifiers against the original document, including examples with leading zeros.

Removing every comma and currency symbol may look convenient, but it hides ambiguity. The strings follow different conventions.

Choose an explicit format per document family. The following parser accepts a deliberately narrow format: ASCII digits, optional correctly grouped thousands commas, a decimal point, and up to two decimal places. It permits a leading minus sign for adjustments.

This intentionally rejects parentheses, currency symbols, exponent notation, and comma-decimal formatting. Those formats may be valid in other documents, but supporting them requires an explicit rule.

Python’s Decimal documentation explains decimal arithmetic. Constructing a Decimal directly from the validated string avoids first introducing a binary floating-point representation.

Practical check: Keep the original extracted value alongside the normalized value, and reconcile the result against other evidence.

A hundred extracted rows are not necessarily the correct hundred rows. One line may be missing while another is duplicated.

Required fields are present and nonempty.

Dates are valid under the declared format.

Line identifiers are unique within the correct scope.

Recognized line-item totals reconcile with the appropriate subtotal.

Each accepted row has a traceable source location.

For a document whose stated subtotal is exactly the sum of its line amounts:

Do not compare that subtotal directly with a grand total containing tax, shipping, or other adjustments. First model those components.

Avoid a generic tolerance such as “accept differences below one dollar.” If the document requires rounding, define where rounding occurs, the currency precision, and the permitted discrepancy.

SitePoint’s overview of data preprocessing provides additional context for separating cleaning, transformation, and integration.

Practical check: Inject one missing row and one duplicate into your fixtures. Confirm that the workflow detects both.

When a record fails validation, a reviewer should not have to search a long PDF without context.

Keep a reference to the source document, page number, extraction run, and original field value. Where the extractor exposes cell coordinates, retain them so a review interface can highlight the relevant region.

Distinguish “not extracted,” “blank in source,” and “not applicable.” Turning all three into an empty string makes it harder to understand what happened.

Confidence scores can help prioritize work, but they are not interchangeable across tools and do not replace business validation. A highly confident extraction can still be placed in the wrong column.

Practical check: Ask someone unfamiliar with the document to resolve a flagged record using only the review interface and its source reference.

An import may stop after extraction, during validation, or while writing records. Retrying should not create another copy of every accepted line.

Assign each import a stable identity. A document hash can help identify byte-identical uploads, while an explicit tenant or account scope prevents unrelated users’ imports from being treated as one.

A hash alone is insufficient for every duplicate policy. Two differently encoded PDFs may represent the same invoice, and one file may legitimately need reprocessing after a parser correction.

Track both the document identity and processing version. Separate extraction attempts from committed business records.

At the database boundary, define the appropriate uniqueness rule and use a transaction for the unit you promise to import atomically. For example, invoice lines might be unique by account, invoice identity, and line number—not by invoice ID alone across all customers.

When reprocessing changes existing values, make that an explicit replacement or correction workflow rather than an unnoticed side effect of retrying.

Practical check: Run the same accepted import twice and verify that the application record count remains unchanged.

The most valuable fixtures are not always the most visually complicated. A tiny change can alter business meaning while producing valid-looking data.

Use pytest parameterization to exercise numeric-format boundarie. SitePoint’s Python unit-testing guide explains the broader testing workflow.

Parser tests do not verify the extraction engine. Add end-to-end fixtures with manually verified expected records for repeated headers, wrapped descriptions, scans, and multi-page tables.

Measure field accuracy and the number of documents that pass all required checks. A strong average can conceal a weak result on the one field your application depends on most.

Practical check: Retain a regression fixture for every meaningful production failure, using synthetic or appropriately sanitized documents.

PDF conversion produces candidate data. Your application decides whether that data is complete, consistent, and suitable for use.

A dependable workflow identifies the source format, preserves extraction evidence, enforces explicit column rules, reconciles values, and makes retries predictable.

Start with one document family and a small verified fixture set. Expand only when you can explain both why a record was accepted and how a reviewer can investigate one that was rejected.

#10767. Electric hypercar wrecks at 280 mph during test, driver returns for even faster run

A nearly 3,000-horsepower electric hypercar crashed during a high-speed test while attempting to reach 280 mph, but its driver escaped without serious injuries before the manufacturer returned for an even faster run.

Chinese automaker BYD shared footage of its Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing into a guardrail during testing, leaving much of the vehicle destroyed while its carbon-fiber cabin remained intact.

The incident comes as BYD prepares to push the electric hypercar beyond its previous top speed of 308 mph, with the company targeting a new record of more than 310 mph.

According to Electrek, the Yangwang U9 Xtreme was undergoing a series of high-speed tests when the accident occurred.

During its first run, the vehicle exceeded 217 mph before reaching more than 261 mph on its second attempt. The third run was intended to push the car beyond 280 mph, but it ended when the hypercar lost control and slammed into a guardrail.

Footage shared by BYD shows the vehicle striking the barrier before spinning across the track, with debris scattering across the road. The front and rear sections sustained extensive damage, although the central carbon-fiber passenger compartment remained intact.

Despite the crash, the driver escaped without serious injuries. BYD confirmed that the driver underwent a comprehensive medical examination at a hospital, where doctors determined they were in good health.

The manufacturer subsequently resumed testing, with another run reaching 284.5 mph, exceeding the speed targeted during the earlier crash. Yangwang representative Jiang Gong said there was still room for improvement and expressed confidence that the vehicle could eventually surpass 310 mph.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is powered by four electric motors producing nearly 3,000 horsepower. It also features a 1,200-volt electrical system and motors capable of reaching 30,000 rpm.

In September 2025, the hypercar reached 308.3 mph during testing in Germany, establishing a new benchmark for production-car top speed.

BYD is now preparing another attempt to exceed 310 mph, with Dubai previously identified as the planned location for a record run in November 2026. However, the company has not confirmed a final date for the attempt.

The automaker ended its crash footage with a message indicating that it intends to continue pursuing higher speeds.

“The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached,” BYD said in a statement translated by Electrek.

#10766. “Existential risk” – Why scientists are racing to define consciousness

As artificial intelligence continues to advance and ethical concerns grow alongside it, scientists say the need to understand consciousness has reached a critical point.

In a new review published in Frontiers in Science, researchers warn that progress in AI and neurotechnology is moving faster than scientific understanding of consciousness. This gap, they argue, could lead to serious ethical problems if it is not addressed.

The authors say explaining how consciousness emerges is now an urgent scientific and moral priority. A clearer understanding could eventually make it possible to develop scientific methods for detecting consciousness. That breakthrough would have far-reaching consequences for AI development, prenatal policy, animal welfare, medicine, mental health care, law, and emerging technologies such as brain-computer interfaces.

"Consciousness science is no longer a purely philosophical pursuit. It has real implications for every facet of society -- and for understanding what it means to be human," said lead author Prof Axel Cleeremans from Université Libre de Bruxelles. "Understanding consciousness is one of the most substantial challenges of 21st-century science -- and it's now urgent due to advances in AI and other technologies.

"If we become able to create consciousness -- even accidentally -- it would raise immense ethical challenges and even existential risk," added Cleeremans, a European Research Council (ERC) grantee.

Consciousness, commonly described as awareness of both the world around us and ourselves, remains one of science's most difficult puzzles. Despite decades of research, scientists still lack agreement on how subjective experience emerges from biological processes.

Researchers have identified brain regions and neural activity linked to conscious experience, but major disagreements remain. Scientists continue to debate which brain systems are truly necessary for consciousness and how they interact to produce awareness. Some researchers even question whether this approach captures the problem correctly.

The new review examines the current state of consciousness science, future directions for the field, and the possible consequences if humans succeed in fully explaining or even creating consciousness. This includes the possibility of consciousness emerging in machines or in lab-grown brain-like systems known as "brain organoids."

The authors argue that developing evidence-based tests for consciousness could transform how awareness is identified across many contexts. Such tools could help detect consciousness in patients with brain injuries or dementia and determine when awareness arises in fetuses, animals, brain organoids, or even AI systems.

While this would represent a major scientific advance, the researchers caution that it would also create difficult ethical and legal questions. Determining that a system is conscious would force society to reconsider how that system should be treated.

"Progress in consciousness science will reshape how we see ourselves and our relationship to both artificial intelligence and the natural world," said co-author Prof Anil Seth from the University of Sussex and ERC grantee. "The question of consciousness is ancient -- but it's never been more urgent than now."

A deeper understanding of consciousness could have wide-ranging effects across society.

In medicine, it could improve care for patients who are unresponsive and assumed to be unconscious. Measurements inspired by integrated information theory and global workspace theory[1] have already detected signs of awareness in some individuals diagnosed with unresponsive wakefulness syndrome. Further progress could refine these tools to better assess consciousness in coma, advanced dementia, and anesthesia, and influence treatment decisions and end-of-life care.

Mental health treatment could also benefit. Understanding the biological basis of subjective experience may help researchers develop better therapies for conditions such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia by narrowing the gap between animal studies and human emotional experience.

Greater insight into consciousness could reshape how humans think about their moral responsibilities toward animals. Identifying which animals and systems are sentient could influence animal research practices, farming, food consumption, and conservation strategies. "Understanding the nature of consciousness in particular animals would transform how we treat them and emerging biological systems that are being synthetically generated by scientists," said co-author Prof Liad Mudrik from Tel Aviv University and ERC grantee.

Consciousness research could also affect how the legal system understands responsibility. New findings may challenge traditional legal concepts such as mens rea, the "guilty mind" required to establish intent. As neuroscience reveals how much behavior arises from unconscious processes, courts may need to reconsider where responsibility begins and ends.

At the same time, advances in AI, brain organoids, and brain-computer interfaces raise the possibility of creating or altering awareness beyond natural biological limits. While some researchers believe consciousness might arise through computation alone, others argue that biological factors play an essential role. "Even if 'conscious AI' is impossible using standard digital computers, AI that gives the impression of being conscious raises many societal and ethical challenges," said Seth.

The authors emphasize the need for a coordinated, evidence-based approach to studying consciousness. One proposed strategy involves adversarial collaborations, in which competing theories are tested against each other through experiments designed jointly by their supporters. "We need more team science to break theoretical silos and overcome existing biases and assumptions," said Mudrik. "This step has the potential to move the field forward."

The researchers also argue that scientific work should place greater emphasis on phenomenology (what consciousness feels like) alongside studies of function (what consciousness does).

"Cooperative efforts are essential to make progress -- and to ensure society is prepared for the ethical, medical, and technological consequences of understanding, and perhaps creating, consciousness," said Cleeremans.

#10763. A tiny light trap could unlock million qubit quantum computers

After years of slow progress, researchers may finally be seeing a clear path forward in the quest to build powerful quantum computers. These machines are expected to dramatically shorten the time required for certain calculations, turning problems that would take classical computers thousands of years into tasks that could be completed in hours.

A team led by physicists at Stanford University has developed a new kind of optical cavity that can efficiently capture single photons, the basic particles of light, emitted by individual atoms. Those atoms serve as the core components of a quantum computer because they store qubits, which are the quantum equivalent of the zeros and ones used in traditional computing. For the first time, this approach allows information to be collected from all qubits at once.

Optical Cavities Enable Faster Qubit Readout

In research published in Nature, the team describes a system made up of 40 optical cavities, each holding a single atom qubit, along with a larger prototype that contains more than 500 cavities. The results point to a realistic route toward building quantum computing networks that could one day include as many as a million qubits.

"If we want to make a quantum computer, we need to be able to read information out of the quantum bits very quickly," said Jon Simon, the study's senior author and associate professor of physics and of applied physics in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "Until now, there hasn't been a practical way to do that at scale because atoms just don't emit light fast enough, and on top of that, they spew it out in all directions. An optical cavity can efficiently guide emitted light toward a particular direction, and now we've found a way to equip each atom in a quantum computer within its own individual cavity."

An optical cavity works by trapping light between two or more reflective surfaces, causing it to bounce back and forth. The effect can be compared to standing between mirrors in a fun house, where reflections seem to stretch endlessly into the distance. In scientific settings, these cavities are far smaller and use repeated passes of a laser beam to extract information from atoms.

Although optical cavities have been studied for decades, they have been difficult to use with atoms because atoms are extremely small and nearly transparent. Getting light to interact with them strongly enough has been a persistent challenge.

Rather than relying on many repeated reflections, the Stanford team introduced microlenses inside each cavity to tightly focus light onto a single atom. Even with fewer light bounces, this method proved more effective at pulling quantum information from the atom.

"We have developed a new type of cavity architecture; it's not just two mirrors anymore," said Adam Shaw, a Stanford Science Fellow and first author on the study. "We hope this will enable us to build dramatically faster, distributed quantum computers that can talk to each other with much faster data rates."

Beyond the Binary Limits of Classical Computing

Conventional computers process information using bits that represent either zero or one. Quantum computers operate using qubits, which are based on the quantum states of tiny particles. A qubit can represent zero, one, or both states at the same time, allowing quantum systems to handle certain calculations far more efficiently than classical machines.

"A classical computer has to churn through possibilities one by one, looking for the correct answer," said Simon. "But a quantum computer acts like noise-canceling headphones that compare combinations of answers, amplifying the right ones while muffling the wrong ones."

Scientists estimate that quantum computers will need millions of qubits to outperform today's most powerful supercomputers. According to Simon, reaching that level will likely require connecting many quantum computers into large networks. The parallel light-based interface demonstrated in this study provides an efficient foundation for scaling up to those sizes.

The researchers showed a working 40-cavity array in the current study, along with a proof-of-concept system containing more than 500 cavities. Their next goal is to expand to tens of thousands. Looking further ahead, the team envisions quantum data centers in which individual quantum computers are linked through cavity-based network interfaces to form full-scale quantum supercomputers.

Broader Scientific and Technological Impact

Significant engineering hurdles remain, but the researchers believe the potential benefits are substantial. Large-scale quantum computers could lead to breakthroughs in materials design and chemical synthesis, including applications related to drug discovery, as well as advances in code breaking.

The ability to efficiently collect light also has implications beyond computing. Cavity arrays could improve biosensing and microscopy, supporting progress in medical and biological research. Quantum networks may even contribute to astronomy by enabling optical telescopes with enhanced resolution, potentially allowing scientists to directly observe planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system.

"As we understand more about how to manipulate light at a single particle level, I think it will transform our ability to see the world," Shaw said.

​​Simon is also the Joan Reinhart Professor of Physics & Applied Physics. Shaw is also a Felix Bloch Fellow and an Urbanek-Chodorow Fellow.

Additional Stanford co-authors include David Schuster, the Joan Reinhart Professor of Applied Physics, and doctoral students Anna Soper, Danial Shadmany, and Da-Yeon Koh.

Other co-authors include researchers from Stony Brook University, the University of Chicago, Harvard University, and Montana State University.

This research received support from the National Science Foundation, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, Army Research Office, Hertz Foundation, and the U.S. Department of Defense.

Matt Jaffe of Montana State University and Simon act as consultants to and hold stock options in Atom Computing. Shadmany, Jaffe, Schuster, and Simon, as well as Aishwarya Kumar of Stony Brook, hold a patent on the resonator geometry demonstrated in this work.

#10760. Scientists create smart synthetic skin that can hide images and change shape

Synthetic materials are widely used across science, engineering, and industry, but most are designed to perform only a narrow range of tasks. A research team at Penn State set out to change that. Led by Hongtao Sun, assistant professor of industrial and manufacturing engineering (IME), the group developed a new fabrication technique that can produce multifunctional "smart synthetic skin." These adaptable materials can be programmed to perform a wide variety of tasks, including hiding or revealing information, enabling adaptive camouflage, and supporting soft robotic systems.

Using this new approach, the researchers created a programmable smart skin made from hydrogel, a soft, water-rich material. Unlike conventional synthetic materials with fixed behaviors, this smart skin can be tuned to respond in multiple ways. Its appearance, mechanical behavior, surface texture, and ability to change shape can all be adjusted when the material is exposed to external triggers such as heat, solvents, or physical stress.

The findings were published in Nature Communications, where the study was also selected for Editors' Highlights.

Inspired by Octopus Skin and Living Systems

Sun, the project's principal investigator, said the concept was inspired by cephalopods such as octopuses, which can rapidly alter the look and texture of their skin. These animals use such changes to blend into their surroundings or communicate with one another.

"Cephalopods use a complex system of muscles and nerves to exhibit dynamic control over the appearance and texture of their skin," Sun said. "Inspired by these soft organisms, we developed a 4D-printing system to capture that idea in a synthetic, soft material."

Sun also holds affiliations in biomedical engineering, material science and engineering, and the Materials Research Institute at Penn State. He described the process as 4D printing because the printed objects are not static. Instead, they can actively change in response to environmental conditions.

Printing Digital Instructions Into Material

To achieve this adaptability, the team used a method called halftone-encoded printing. This technique converts image or texture data into binary ones and zeros and embeds that information directly into the material. The approach is similar to how dot patterns are used in newspapers or photographs to create images.

By encoding these digital patterns within the hydrogel, the researchers can program how the smart skin reacts to different stimuli. The printed patterns determine how various regions of the material respond. Some areas may swell, shrink, or soften more than others when exposed to temperature changes, liquids, or mechanical forces. By carefully designing these patterns, the team can control the material's overall behavior.

"In simple terms, we're printing instructions into the material," Sun explained. "Those instructions tell the skin how to react when something changes around it."

One of the most eye-catching demonstrations involved the material's ability to conceal and reveal visual information. Haoqing Yang, a doctoral candidate in IME and the paper's first author, said this capability highlights the potential of the smart skin.

To demonstrate the effect, the team encoded an image of the Mona Lisa into the hydrogel film. When the material was washed with ethanol, it appeared transparent and showed no visible image. The hidden image became clear only after the film was placed in ice water or gradually heated.

Yang noted that the Mona Lisa was used only as an example. The printing technique allows virtually any image to be encoded into the hydrogel.

"This behavior could be used for camouflage, where a surface blends into its environment, or for information encryption, where messages are hidden and only revealed under specific conditions," Yang said.

The researchers also showed that concealed patterns could be detected by gently stretching the material and analyzing how it deforms using digital image correlation analysis. This means information can be revealed not only visually, but also through mechanical interaction, adding an extra level of security.

The smart skin also demonstrated remarkable flexibility. According to Sun, the material can easily shift from a flat sheet into complex, bio-inspired shapes with detailed surface textures. Unlike many other shape-changing materials, this transformation does not require multiple layers or different substances.

Instead, the changes in shape and texture are controlled entirely by the digitally printed halftone patterns within a single sheet. This allows the material to replicate effects similar to those seen in cephalopod skin.

Building on this capability, the team showed that multiple functions can be programmed to work together. By carefully designing the halftone patterns, they encoded the Mona Lisa image into flat films that later transformed into three-dimensional forms. As the sheets curved into dome-like shapes, the hidden image slowly appeared, showing that changes in shape and visual appearance can be coordinated within one material.

"Similar to how cephalopods coordinate body shape and skin patterning, the synthetic smart skin can simultaneously control what it looks like and how it deforms, all within a single, soft material," Sun said.

Expanding the Potential of 4D-Printed Hydrogels

Sun said the new work builds on earlier research by the team on 4D-printed smart hydrogels, which was also published in Nature Communications. That earlier study focused on combining mechanical properties with programmable transitions from flat to three-dimensional forms. In the current research, the team expanded the approach by using halftone-encoded 4D printing to integrate even more functions into a single hydrogel film.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to create a scalable and versatile platform that allows precise digital encoding of multiple functions within one adaptive material.

"This interdisciplinary research at the intersection of advanced manufacturing, intelligent materials and mechanics opens new opportunities with broad implications for stimulus-responsive systems, biomimetic engineering, advanced encryption technologies, biomedical devices and more," Sun said.

The study also included Penn State co-authors Haotian Li and Juchen Zhang, both doctoral candidates in IME, and Tengxiao Liu, a lecturer in biomedical engineering. H. Jerry Qi, professor of mechanical engineering at Georgia Institute of Technology, also collaborated on the project.

#10758. Beyond the Password Reset: Building Recovery Experiences That Protect Online Shopping

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An unfamiliar delivery address appears in a shopper’s account. Minutes later, an order confirmation arrives for something they never purchased. They try to sign in, but their password no longer works.

For the consumer, this is an urgent problem: stop the misuse, recover access, and understand what happened. For developers, it exposes a gap between building a login screen and building a service that remains useful when that login is compromised.

This article examines recovery from a business-to-consumer perspective: what an individual shopper needs, and how developers can translate those needs into safer interfaces and backend controls.

Account takeover and identity theft can overlap, but they are different problems.

Account takeover means someone has gained unauthorized control of an existing account. Identity theft involves misuse of someone’s personal information. Recovering access to one shopping account does not necessarily resolve misuse elsewhere.

Design the interface around questions a worried customer can answer:

A recovery page should explain the scope of help. “Recover your shopping account” is a specific promise. “Restore your identity” describes a much broader outcome that an ordinary retailer cannot deliver on its own.

Before building the workflow, list the consumer-visible assets involved: account access, addresses, order history, payment references, contact details, and support messages. Each needs its own review or remediation step.

A shopper who cannot sign in must still be able to locate help. Provide a public “My account may be compromised” entry point alongside ordinary password recovery.

Separate the two journeys. Someone who forgot a password usually needs a credential reset. Someone reporting suspicious activity may also need unauthorized changes reversed, orders investigated, and existing access revoked.

Avoid using a submitted email address as proof of ownership. A public report can initiate triage, but it should not expose order history or authorize sensitive changes.

OWASP’s Forgot Password Cheat Sheet recommends consistent responses for existing and nonexistent accounts, rate limiting, and securely generated reset tokens that expire and work only once.

If the details match an account, we’ll send instructions through an available recovery method.

The frontend message is only one part of that protection. Different response timing or API behavior can still reveal account existence.

After verifying a recovery factor, resist granting immediate access to every account feature.

A useful architecture gives the consumer a short-lived recovery session with narrowly defined permissions. For example, it might permit reviewing security settings while preventing purchases, data exports, or changes to payment information.

This type documents intent; it does not enforce security. The server must validate the session, its expiry, its association with the account, and the required permission on every request.

Check resource ownership separately. Permission to request an order review must never allow a consumer to submit another customer’s order identifier.

Do not treat an attacker’s recently changed email address as trustworthy recovery evidence. Review recovery options against previously established evidence and the account’s required level of assurance.

A new password is insufficient if an attacker still holds a valid session.

OWASP’s compromise-recovery guidance calls for reviewing recovery contacts and authentication methods, removing unauthorized changes, and invalidating existing sessions and outstanding recovery credentials after successful recovery.

For a consumer application, translate that into a visible checklist:

Use a durable workflow so a partial failure cannot silently appear as completion. Credential replacement and session revocation may span different systems; record pending work, retry failed operations safely, and show the consumer an accurate status.

JWT-based applications need particular care. Changing a password does not automatically invalidate an independently verifiable token. Choose an enforceable revocation strategy, such as checking a server-side session record or account security version on protected requests.

The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet provides background on session lifecycle controls.

Recovery screens are often used on a phone, in a hurry, by someone who is uncertain about what happened.

Use short steps with clear outcomes: “Review recent changes,” “Secure your sign-in,” and “Check your orders.” Explain why information is requested before asking for it.

Use native form controls with visible labels. Associate field instructions and errors with their inputs, keep keyboard navigation predictable, and move focus deliberately when a step changes. SitePoint’s HTML Form Elements guide is useful background for building these controls.

A simple reporting form might begin with:

Provide an alternative when the consumer cannot access their usual inbox. That alternative needs its own verification process; support staff should not bypass security simply because a caller sounds convincing.

Once the immediate account problem is contained, a consumer may need help addressing misuse of personal information elsewhere.

Keep this guidance separate from the application’s own recovery controls. A retailer can investigate its orders and secure its accounts. It cannot directly correct records held by unrelated organizations.

For U.S. consumers, link to the FTC’s IdentityTheft.gov as a government resource. Offer country-appropriate resources when serving other regions.

Consumers considering paid assistance can also review an identity recovery service to understand the support available for broader restoration tasks. They should check eligibility, exclusions, and service terms before relying on it.

External assistance should remain optional. Restoring access to a customer’s account should not depend on purchasing another product.

Consumers need an understandable record of what happened. Offer a case summary with relevant timestamps, reported changes, affected orders, completed actions, and unresolved questions.

Separate customer-facing information from internal investigation details. A consumer may need to know that an address changed; they do not need raw authentication tokens or internal fraud-detection rules.

Treat recovery data as sensitive. Avoid recording passwords, recovery secrets, or full payment details in logs. Restrict staff access to case information and define retention periods appropriate to its purpose.

If evidence uploads are necessary, provide a secured upload route with access controls and a deletion policy. Do not ask customers to send sensitive documents to an ordinary support inbox by default.

A successful redirect is a weak definition of recovery.

After recovery, help consumers strengthen their sign-in. SitePoint’s Developer Guide to Implementing Passkeys offers a starting point for exploring passkey authentication.

A stronger sign-in method still needs a carefully designed fallback. Evaluate the recovery path whenever you change authentication.

For a shopper, recovery succeeds when unauthorized access stops, legitimate access returns, and the next steps are clear.

Developers can support that outcome by treating recovery as a complete product journey: limited permissions, enforceable revocation, accessible interfaces, accurate case status, and clear boundaries around external assistance.

The most useful question in a design review is simple: if this were your account, could you regain control and tell what still needs attention?

#10755. AI reads brain MRIs in seconds and flags emergencies

A newly developed artificial intelligence system from the University of Michigan can analyze brain MRI scans and deliver a diagnosis in a matter of seconds, according to a new study. The model identified neurological conditions with accuracy reaching 97.5% and was also able to assess how urgently patients needed medical care.

Researchers say this first-of-its-kind technology has the potential to reshape how brain imaging is handled across health systems in the United States. The findings were published in Nature Biomedical Engineering.

"As the global demand for MRI rises and places significant strain our physicians and health systems, our AI model has potential to reduce burden by improving diagnosis and treatment with fast, accurate information," said senior author Todd Hollon, M.D., a neurosurgeon at University of Michigan Health and assistant professor of neurosurgery at U-M Medical School.

Hollon named the new technology Prima. Over a one-year period, his research team evaluated the system using more than 30,000 MRI studies.

Across more than 50 different radiologic diagnoses involving major neurological disorders, Prima delivered stronger diagnostic performance than other advanced AI models. In addition to identifying disease, the system also proved capable of determining which cases required higher priority.

Certain neurological conditions, including strokes and brain hemorrhages, demand immediate medical attention. Hollon said that in these situations, Prima can automatically alert health care providers so action can be taken quickly.

The system was designed to notify the most appropriate subspecialist, such as a stroke neurologist or neurosurgeon. Feedback becomes available immediately after a patient completes imaging.

"Accuracy is paramount when reading a brain MRI, but quick turnaround times are critical for timely diagnosis and improved outcomes," said Yiwei Lyu, M.S., co-first author and postdoctoral fellow of Computer Science and Engineering at U-M.

"At key steps in the process, our results show how Prima can improve workflows and streamline clinical care without abandoning accuracy."

Prima is classified as a vision language model (VLM), a type of artificial intelligence that can process images, video, and text together in real time. While artificial intelligence has been applied to MRI analysis before, researchers say Prima takes a different approach.

Earlier models were typically trained on carefully selected subsets of MRI data and designed to perform narrow tasks, such as identifying lesions or estimating dementia risk. Prima was trained on a much broader dataset.

Hollon's team used every available MRI collected since radiology records were digitized at University of Michigan Health. This included more than 200,000 MRI studies and 5.6 million imaging sequences. The model also incorporated patients' clinical histories and the reasons physicians ordered each imaging study.

"Prima works like a radiologist by integrating information regarding the patient's medical history and imaging data to produce a comprehensive understanding of their health," said co-first author Samir Harake, a data scientist in Hollon's Machine Learning in Neurosurgery Lab.

"This enables better performance across a broad range of prediction tasks."

Addressing MRI Delays and Radiology Shortages

Each year, millions of MRI scans are performed worldwide, many of them focused on neurological disease. Researchers say the demand for these scans is growing faster than the availability of neuroradiology services.

This imbalance has contributed to staffing shortages, diagnostic delays, and errors. Depending on where a patient receives a scan, results may take days or even longer to return.

"Whether you are receiving a scan at a larger health system that is facing increasing volume or a rural hospital with limited resources, innovative technologies are needed to improve access to radiology services," said Vikas Gulani, M.D. Ph.D., co-author and chair of the Department of Radiology at U-M Health.

"Our teams at University of Michigan have collaborated to develop a cutting-edge solution to this problem with tremendous, scalable potential."

Although Prima performed strongly, researchers emphasize that the work is still in an early evaluation phase. Future research will focus on incorporating more detailed patient information and electronic medical record data to further improve diagnostic accuracy.

This approach mirrors how radiologists and physicians interpret MRIs and other imaging studies in real clinical settings. While artificial intelligence is already used in health care, most existing systems are limited to narrowly defined tasks.

Hollon describes Prima as "ChatGPT for medical imaging," noting that similar technology could eventually be adapted for other imaging types, including mammograms, chest X-rays and ultrasounds.

"Like the way AI tools can help draft an email or provide recommendations, Prima aims to be a co-pilot for interpreting medical imaging studies," Hollon said.

"We believe that Prima exemplifies the transformative potential of integrating health systems and AI-driven models to improve health care through innovation."

Additional authors: Asadur Chowdury, M.S., Soumyanil Banerjee, M.S., Rachel Gologorsky, Shixuan Liu, Anna-Katharina Meissner, M.D., Akshay Rao, Chenhui Zhao, Akhil Kondepudi, Cheng Jiang, Xinhai Hou, Rushikesh S. Joshi, M.D., Volker Neuschmelting, M.D., Ashok Srinivasan, M.D., Dawn Kleindorfer, M.D., Brian Athey, Ph.D., Aditya Pandey, M.D., and Honglak Lee, Ph.D., all of University of Michigan.

Funding/disclosures: This work was supported in part by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (K12NS080223) of the National Institutes of Health.

The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the NIH.

This work was also supported by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), Frankel Institute for Heart and Brain Health, the Mark Trauner Brain Research Fund, the Zenkel Family Foundation, Ian's Friends Foundation and the UM Precision Health Investigators Awards grant program.

#10754. Italian chef fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza

An Italian chef has been fired from a pizza restaurant in Australia after refusing to customize a pizza for a customer and put pineapple on it for their order.

There have been some divisive pizza toppings over the years, but the debate around putting pineapple on pizza is the fiercest. Some pizza restaurants see it as sacrilege and refuse to do it, while others are happy to serve up a Hawaiian slice to customers.

Over in Queensland, Australia, the La Costa restaurant – which is now closed – fired chef Davide Tamburella following a string of complaints from customers. One complaint, however, has caught attention more than others.

As per the BBC, reporting on a case from Australia’s Fair Work Commission, the chef refused to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a private function.

According to the report, Tamburella refused to take direction and make the pizza as it “need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture”.

The Fair Work Commission was told that “he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture” and had previously told his boss to “check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza”.

Tamburella lost his unfair dismissal claim as it was filed too late in the day, as per the BBC, but also “acknowledged use of inappropriate language and escalation of the situation during service.”

Elliot Ingram, managing director of La Costa Restaurant and Bar, told the Daily Mail there was “more to this story than a pizza topping” too, hinting at other complaints being made about the chef.

It wasn’t the first time that the chef had refused to make the custom pizza either. As per the report, he’d actually done it three times in four years.

#10752. Brain inspired machines are better at math than expected

Computers designed to mimic the structure of the human brain are showing an unexpected strength. They can solve some of the demanding mathematical equations that lie at the heart of major scientific and engineering problems.

In a study published in Nature Machine Intelligence, Sandia National Laboratories computational neuroscientists Brad Theilman and Brad Aimone introduced a new algorithm that allows neuromorphic hardware to solve partial differential equations, or PDEs -- the mathematical foundation for modeling phenomena such as fluid dynamics, electromagnetic fields and structural mechanics.

The results demonstrate that neuromorphic systems can handle these equations efficiently. The advance could help open the door to the first neuromorphic supercomputer, offering a new path toward energy efficient computing for national security and other critical applications.

The research was funded by the Department of Energy's Office of Science through the Advanced Scientific Computing Research and Basic Energy Sciences programs, as well as the National Nuclear Security Administration's Advanced Simulation and Computing program.

Solving Partial Differential Equations With Brain Like Hardware

Partial differential equations are essential for simulating real world systems. They are used to forecast weather, analyze how materials respond to stress, and model complex physical processes. Traditionally, solving PDEs requires enormous computing power. Neuromorphic computers approach the problem differently by processing information in ways that resemble how the brain operates.

"We're just starting to have computational systems that can exhibit intelligent-like behavior. But they look nothing like the brain, and the amount of resources that they require is ridiculous, frankly," Theilman said.

For years, neuromorphic systems were mainly viewed as tools for pattern recognition or for speeding up artificial neural networks. Few expected them to manage mathematically rigorous problems such as PDEs, which are typically handled by large scale supercomputers.

Aimone and Theilman were not surprised by the outcome. They argue that the human brain routinely carries out highly complex calculations, even if people are unaware of it.

"Pick any sort of motor control task -- like hitting a tennis ball or swinging a bat at a baseball," Aimone said. "These are very sophisticated computations. They are exascale-level problems that our brains are capable of doing very cheaply."

Energy Efficient Computing for National Security

The findings could have major implications for the National Nuclear Security Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the nation's nuclear deterrent. Supercomputers used across the nuclear weapons complex consume vast amounts of electricity to simulate the physics of nuclear systems and other high stakes scenarios.

Neuromorphic computing may provide a way to significantly cut energy use while still delivering strong computational performance. By solving PDEs in a brain inspired manner, these systems suggest that large simulations could be run using far less power than conventional supercomputers require.

"You can solve real physics problems with brain-like computation," Aimone said. "That's something you wouldn't expect because people's intuition goes the opposite way. And in fact, that intuition is often wrong."

The team envisions neuromorphic supercomputers eventually becoming central to Sandia's mission of protecting national security.

What Neuromorphic Computing Reveals About the Brain

Beyond engineering advances, the research also touches on deeper questions about intelligence and how the brain performs calculations. The algorithm developed by Theilman and Aimone closely mirrors the structure and behavior of cortical networks.

"We based our circuit on a relatively well-known model in the computational neuroscience world," Theilman said. "We've shown the model has a natural but non-obvious link to PDEs, and that link hasn't been made until now -- 12 years after the model was introduced."

The researchers believe this work could help connect neuroscience with applied mathematics, offering new understanding of how the brain processes information.

"Diseases of the brain could be diseases of computation," Aimone said. "But we don't have a solid grasp on how the brain performs computations yet."

If that idea proves correct, neuromorphic computing might one day contribute to better understanding and treatment of neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

Building the Next Generation of Supercomputers

Neuromorphic computing remains an emerging field, but this work represents an important step forward. The Sandia team hopes their results will encourage collaboration among mathematicians, neuroscientists and engineers to expand what this technology can achieve.

"If we've already shown that we can import this relatively basic but fundamental applied math algorithm into neuromorphic -- is there a corresponding neuromorphic formulation for even more advanced applied math techniques?" Theilman said.

As development continues, the researchers are optimistic. "We have a foot in the door for understanding the scientific questions, but also we have something that solves a real problem," Theilman said.

Choosing the best 3D animation software depends on your experience, budget, and creative goals. Some tools offer complete 3D modeling and animation workflows, while others specialize in professional character animation, visual effects, or AI-powered video creation. This guide compares five options and notes how each fits into web and game projects, so designers and developers can see which one suits their pipeline.

Blender is one of the strongest free options for anyone looking for comprehensive 3D animation software. This open-source application combines modeling, sculpting, rigging, animation, rendering, simulation, and compositing in one package.

Blender provides a broad production workflow without requiring users to pay for a standard commercial license. Its active community, learning resources, and add-on ecosystem make it accessible to independent creators. It is suitable for everything from simple animated scenes to complex short films and game assets.

For web and game developers: Blender ships with a glTF 2.0 importer and exporter, and glTF is the format libraries such as three.js load for 3D on the web. See the Blender manual’s glTF page for export options.

Its extensive interface and feature set can feel overwhelming to new users. Learning advanced rigging, lighting, materials, and rendering takes time, and some established studios may have specialized pipelines built around other applications.

Beginners, freelancers, indie game developers, students, and professionals who need a powerful 3D animation tool without a software subscription.

Autodesk Maya is a professional 3D application widely associated with character animation, rigging, film production, and game development. It offers detailed control over character movement and complex animation workflows, making it a strong choice for artists working in established production environments.

Maya provides sophisticated tools for animating characters and managing complex scenes. Its established role in many professional workflows makes it a valuable skill for artists pursuing careers in film, television, and game development. It also offers detailed control over animation timing, character motion, and rig behavior.

Maya generally requires a paid subscription, which can be expensive for hobbyists and independent creators. Its advanced interface also takes time to learn, particularly for users who have never worked with professional 3D software.

Professional animators, film and television artists, game studios, and users who need advanced character animation and rigging capabilities.

Cinema 4D is a 3D modeling, animation, and rendering application known for its motion graphics workflow. It is widely used for commercial visuals, broadcast graphics, product animations, and creative work that combines 3D elements with graphic design.

Cinema 4D is a strong option for designers who want to create polished motion graphics and branded animation. Its MoGraph workflow can make repetitive or complex movements easier to manage, and its integration with common design workflows is helpful for agencies and creative teams.

For web and product designers: Cinema 4D includes a glTF exporter, which helps when a designer needs to hand a 3D model to a developer for the web. Maxon documents the options on its glTF export settings page.

Cinema 4D is a commercial product, so ongoing licensing costs may be a concern. Although it can handle a wide range of 3D work, users focused on highly specialized character animation or procedural visual effects may prefer tools designed around those workflows.

Motion designers, advertising agencies, broadcast artists, product visualization specialists, and creators who regularly produce animated graphics.

Houdini, developed by SideFX, is a 3D software package known for procedural workflows and advanced visual effects. Rather than relying entirely on manually created steps, artists can build systems that generate and modify complex scenes, simulations, and effects.

Houdini offers exceptional flexibility for technical artists and visual-effects specialists. Procedural workflows make it possible to create reusable systems and adjust complex effects efficiently. Its capabilities are particularly valuable when a project needs detailed simulations or large numbers of interconnected elements.

For game developers: SideFX offers Houdini Engine plugins for Unity and Unreal Engine, which let procedural Houdini assets be used inside those engines. SideFX explains the plugins in its Houdini Engine FAQ.

Houdini has a steep learning curve, especially for beginners who are unfamiliar with node-based workflows. Building effective procedural systems requires patience and technical understanding. While free learning options are available, some commercial uses and advanced workflows require an appropriate paid license.

Visual-effects artists, technical directors, simulation specialists, and experienced 3D creators working on demanding film, television, or game projects.

MagicLight.AI is different from the four tools above. It is an AI-powered video creation platform rather than a traditional 3D application, so it produces finished animated videos, not editable 3D scenes, rigs, or game assets. It is included here for readers who want animated storytelling without building a 3D pipeline. It supports AI-generated characters, scene creation, storyboarding, and voice features.

MagicLight.AI can reduce the time and technical effort needed to create animated videos. It is particularly useful for content creators, educators, marketers, and storytellers who want to focus on the script and final message rather than mastering a complex 3D production pipeline.

MagicLight.AI is not a replacement for dedicated 3D software when you need precise control over mesh topology, character rigs, keyframes, physics, or custom 3D scenes. Creators who need editable 3D assets for games or studio production will need a conventional 3D application such as the ones above.

Content creators, educators, and marketers who want to produce animated videos efficiently without learning a traditional 3D animation workflow.

The right software is the one that supports your actual production needs. Before choosing a tool, consider the following factors.

If you want to model objects, build character rigs, and control animation precisely, start with a dedicated 3D application such as Blender or Maya. If your goal is to create animated storytelling videos from scripts or ideas with less manual production work, an AI video tool such as MagicLight.AI may be a more convenient option.

Blender is an excellent starting point if you need a complete 3D toolset without a standard license fee. Houdini also has a free Apprentice edition with restrictions. Maya and Cinema 4D are commercial applications, so compare their current plans against your expected usage before committing.

Different applications suit different workflows. Blender is versatile, Maya excels at character animation, Cinema 4D is well suited to motion graphics, and Houdini is especially powerful for procedural effects. MagicLight.AI is better suited to AI-assisted video production than to detailed, manually controlled 3D scene creation.

Beginners may find Blender’s extensive learning resources helpful, although its broad feature set takes time to master. Maya and Houdini demand more specialized skills for advanced work, while Cinema 4D is often considered by motion designers seeking a more direct design-oriented workflow. AI video tools can reduce the amount of technical setup required, but still require creative direction and review.

Think about where the finished animation will be used. A web project may need a lightweight glTF model. A game project may require exportable 3D assets, rig compatibility, and a game-engine workflow. A commercial motion graphic may depend on rendering and compositing integration. A social video or animated explainer may prioritize turnaround time, narration, subtitles, and scene continuity.

The best 3D animation software in 2026 depends on your budget, experience, and intended output. Blender is the strongest starting point for many users who want a comprehensive free 3D workflow. Autodesk Maya is a compelling option for professional character animation, Cinema 4D suits motion graphics and commercial visuals, and Houdini stands out for procedural effects and complex simulations. MagicLight.AI offers a different approach: it helps creators generate animated videos with AI rather than manually building a traditional 3D production pipeline.

Blender is one of the best free options because it includes modeling, rigging, animation, rendering, and other production tools in a single open-source application. It is suitable for beginners as well as experienced artists.

Yes. Free software can support professional-quality work when used effectively. Blender, for example, provides a comprehensive toolset for animation and rendering. The final result depends on the artist’s skills, project requirements, hardware, and production workflow.

Blender is a strong choice for beginners who want to learn traditional 3D modeling and animation without paying for a standard software license. Those who mainly want to create animated videos from stories or scripts may prefer exploring an AI video creation platform such as MagicLight.AI.

Blender and Cinema 4D can both export glTF, a format widely used for 3D on the web. Blender is free, so it is the easiest place to start.

#10748. Quantum computer breakthrough tracks qubit fluctuations in real time

Researchers at the Niels Bohr Institute have significantly increased how quickly changes in delicate quantum states can be detected inside a qubit. By combining commercially available hardware with new adaptive measurement techniques, the team can now observe rapid shifts in qubit behavior that were previously impossible to see.

Qubits are the fundamental units of quantum computers, which scientists hope will one day outperform today's most powerful machines. But qubits are extremely sensitive. The materials used to build them often contain tiny defects that scientists still do not fully understand. These microscopic imperfections can shift position hundreds of times per second. As they move, they alter how quickly a qubit loses energy and with it valuable quantum information.

Until recently, standard testing methods took up to a minute to measure qubit performance. That was far too slow to capture these rapid fluctuations. Instead, researchers could only determine an average energy loss rate, masking the true and often unstable behavior of the qubit.

It is somewhat like asking a strong workhorse to pull a plow while obstacles constantly appear in its path faster than anyone can react. The animal may be capable, but unpredictable disruptions make the job much harder.

A research team from the Niels Bohr Institute's Center for Quantum Devices and the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme, led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Fabrizio Berritta, developed a real time adaptive measurement system that tracks changes in the qubit energy loss (relaxation) rate as they occur. The project involved collaboration with scientists from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Leiden University, and Chalmers University.

The new approach relies on a fast classical controller that updates its estimate of a qubit's relaxation rate within milliseconds. This matches the natural speed of the fluctuations themselves, rather than lagging seconds or minutes behind as older methods did.

To achieve this, the team used a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a type of classical processor designed for extremely rapid operations. By running the experiment directly on the FPGA, they could quickly generate a "best guess" of how fast the qubit was losing energy using only a few measurements. This eliminated the need for slower data transfers to a conventional computer.

Programming FPGAs for such specialized tasks can be challenging. Even so, the researchers succeeded in updating the controller's internal Bayesian model after every single qubit measurement. That allowed the system to continually refine its understanding of the qubit's condition in real time.

As a result, the controller now keeps pace with the qubit's changing environment. Measurements and adjustments happen on nearly the same timescale as the fluctuations themselves, making the system roughly one hundred times faster than previously demonstrated.

The work also revealed something new. Scientists did not previously know just how quickly fluctuations occur in superconducting qubits. These experiments have now provided that insight.

Commercial Quantum Hardware Meets Advanced Control

FPGAs have long been used in other scientific and engineering fields. In this case, the researchers used a commercially available FPGA based controller from Quantum Machines called the OPX1000. The system can be programmed in a language similar to Python, which many physicists already use, making it more accessible to research groups worldwide.

The integration of this controller with advanced quantum hardware was made possible through close collaboration between the Niels Bohr Institute research group led by Associate Professor Morten Kjaergaard and Chalmers University, where the quantum processing unit was designed and fabricated. "The controller enables very tight integration between logic, measurements and feedforward: these components made our experiment possible," says Morten Kjærgaard.

Why Real Time Calibration Matters for Quantum Computers

Quantum technologies promise powerful new capabilities, though practical large scale quantum computers are still under development. Progress often comes incrementally, but occasionally major steps forward occur.

By uncovering these previously hidden dynamics, the findings reshape how scientists think about testing and calibrating superconducting quantum processors. With current materials and manufacturing methods, moving toward real time monitoring and adjustment appears essential for improving reliability. The results also highlight the importance of partnerships between academic research and industry, along with creative uses of available technology.

"Nowadays, in quantum processing units in general, the overall performance is not determined by the best qubits, but by the worst ones: those are the ones we need to focus on. The surprise from our work is that a 'good' qubit can turn into a 'bad' one in fractions of a second, rather than minutes or hours.

"With our algorithm, the fast control hardware can pinpoint which qubit is 'good' or 'bad' basically in real time. We can also gather useful statistics on the 'bad` qubits in seconds instead of hours or days.

"We still cannot explain a large fraction of the fluctuations we observe. Understanding and controlling the physics behind such fluctuations in qubit properties will be necessary for scaling quantum processors to a useful size," Fabrizio says.
